regime_line: The buyback reprieve lasted exactly one session: a blowout Philly Fed (47.4 vs. a consensus near 24) put the long-end selloff back on — 30Y +4bp to 5.23%, re-flagged at +1.8σ — while Walmart printed its slowest sales growth in six-plus years and the tape de-risked broadly, with AI hardware, of all things, catching the bid.

claims_section_html:
Claims ledger

  • CL-0001 (hawkish minutes → 30Y above 5.31) — deadline is today's close. Thursday closed 5.23%, 8bp short of the trigger with one session left — and note the test got its best shot: the data came in hot (Philly Fed 47.4) and the long end still only recovered half of Wednesday's buyback drop. Final grade in Monday's brief, on today's close.
  • CL-0002 (rate-rotation, not AI-demand doubt) — interim: recovering. SMH outperformed SPY by +1.15pp Thursday (+0.31% vs. −0.84%) on a broad down day, clawing the cumulative tally back to −0.61pp of the −2pp refutation threshold, day 2 of 5. Hardware rallying while the index falls is exactly what the rotation hypothesis predicts on the round trip. Due 08-25.
  • CL-0003 (real-rate/term-premium story) — interim: holding. Breakeven 2.30% (≤ 2.35 ✓), 10Y 4.69% (≥ 4.60 ✓). Thursday's rise came alongside a hot growth print with breakevens flat — still a price-of-time story, not an inflation story. Due 08-25.
  • CL-0004 (new, due 08-28): Walmart's print signals broadening consumer softness rather than company-specific share loss — test: Consumer Discretionary (XLY) underperforms SPX by ≥ 1.5pp cumulative over the next 5 trading days. Deere and Estée Lauder beat the same week, so the soft-consumer reading is a hypothesis, not a fact — hence the ledger.
story_html:
Wednesday's story died on Thursday's data. Initial jobless claims came in at 206K against 210K expected (Reuters/Investing.com) and the Philadelphia Fed's manufacturing index printed 47.4 against a consensus near 24 — a blowout regional factory reading that, as coverage put it, "reinforced the case for the Fed to stay put" (Babypips). The long end gave back half of the buyback rally in one session: 30Y +4bp to 5.23%, 10Y +4bp to 4.69%, and the 30Y is re-flagged at +1.8σ this morning. The lesson the ledger will record: a supply intervention can cap the long end for a day, but the price of long money is still being set by the data — and the data ran hot.

The equity tape confirmed the regime shift in its own way. All four majors closed lower (S&P −0.87%, Russell −1.34%) and — for the first day since this system began — no sector tripped the ±1.5pp divergence screen: Tuesday and Wednesday were rotation days with clear winners; Thursday was uniform de-risking. The headline casualty was Walmart, down 9.15% after reporting its slowest quarterly sales growth in more than six years (Yahoo Finance, Nasdaq.com) — the week's first genuinely soft consumer datapoint, now logged as CL-0004 rather than swallowed as a conclusion, because the same week produced beats from Estée Lauder and Deere.

The counter-current worth noticing: AI hardware outperformed on a red day — SMH +0.31% against the S&P's −0.87%, with Lumentum +6.25% and Marvell +5.79% bouncing — precisely when the discount-rate excuse for selling it returned. That is the behavior CL-0002 predicted, and it moves the evidence away from "the market is repricing AI demand" and back toward "last week's crowding got unwound, fast." Credit spent the whole drama asleep: HY OAS 2.73% (z −0.7), IG 0.81%. Nothing in this week says stress; everything says the price of time is being renegotiated in public.

dashboard_interp_html: The week's whole drama lives in one row: the 30Y has gone 5.31 → 5.19 → 5.23 in three sessions — term-premium spike, buyback relief, hot-data giveback — while the 2Y sat at 4.19% through all of it. That front-end stillness is the tell that none of this has been about the Fed's path. The real 10Y eased to 2.35% (Wednesday's print, z +1.2) with breakevens flat at 2.30%, keeping CL-0003 intact. The weekly H.4.1 confirms the backdrop: the balance sheet shrank $14.3B to $6.746T, TGA eased $10.3B to $954B, ON RRP sits at $0.2B — QT grinding on with the buffer gone, which is exactly why long-end supply announcements now move the market more than Fed minutes do. Equal-weight remains flagged (+1.6σ) even after Thursday's dip: breadth bent, didn't break.

Mechanical screens, 2026-08-20 close: 502/502 S&P constituents scanned; 29 name candidates; no sector divergence ≥ 1.5pp (first screen-empty day for the sector rule — itself information). Earnings reactions prioritized per §5. Stated reasons are attributed reporting, not asserted causes; Bigdata.com still down, gap per §4.

WMT −9.15% (103.84, from 114.30) — the fact: a top-20 market cap's worst day of the year, on earnings. Stated reason: slowest quarterly sales growth in more than six years (Yahoo Finance, Nasdaq.com coverage of the Q2 report). Read-through: the highest-signal consumer datapoint of the week, from the retailer closest to the median household — but one print against Estée Lauder's beat and TJX's sector strength is a divergence to test, not a verdict. CL-0004 gives it a falsifiable form; the client-conversation version is below.

MRNA −23.55% (133.32, from 174.38) — the fact: gave back roughly a quarter of its value the day after the century's largest S&P gain. Stated reason: profit-taking on Wednesday's cancer-vaccine rally; analysts flagged more volatility ahead (Seeking Alpha). Read-through: idiosyncratic — no read-through beyond the mechanics lesson: the two-day round trip (+177%, −24%) is what price discovery after a binary event looks like, and it will be the week's most-asked client question alongside Walmart.

DE +6.94% (620.94, from 580.63) — the fact: best day among earnings reporters. Stated reason: Q3 profit of $1.38B on revenue up 5% to $12.6B, both above expectations, with the low end of full-year guidance raised; construction & forestry sales +18% while its largest division, production agriculture, slipped 6% (Bloomberg, GuruFocus). Read-through: the industrial-capex side of the economy is doing fine — construction equipment +18% rhymes with the hot Philly Fed — while big-row-crop agriculture stays in recession. Strength with that internal split supports "resilient economy, selective softness," the same shape Walmart-vs-Deere paints at the consumer/industrial level.

Sector note: none qualified — no GICS sector ETF diverged ≥ 1.5pp from SPX, the first empty screen since the system began. After two days of violent rotation, Thursday's selling was uniform: that is de-risking into a hot-data print, not a leadership change.

tier3_html:
Weekly review (Friday depth): the week in one arc — SMH underperformed SPY by 3.4pp Tuesday and 1.8pp Wednesday, then outperformed by 1.15pp Thursday while the index fell; YTD the complex still leads +56.2% to +11.8%. Dispersion inside the complex was the week's texture: optics and storage collapsed early (COHR −12.8% Tuesday, STX −16.3% over two days) while Thursday's bounce was led by the same tier (LITE +6.25%, MRVL +5.79%). A crowded trade was violently de-grossed and partially re-bought inside four sessions — positioning, on the evidence so far, not a demand event. CL-0002 formalizes that judgment and resolves Tuesday.

Financing-cycle health: no new AI-adjacent issuance or structure news surfaced through available channels this week; the standing item remains BofA's $370B sizing of Broadcom's XPV leasing vehicle (routed to NR on 08-19). The cycle-level scoreboard this week: equity-side repricing of the hardware complex, zero response in credit (HY OAS 2.73%, near YTD lows), and no visible pullback in announced financing. That combination — equity volatility with credit indifference — is early-cycle behavior on the financing-cycle map, not late; the section's job is to notice when credit stops being indifferent.

Liquidity panel (weekly): balance sheet $6.746T (−$14.3B w/w, QT ongoing), TGA $954B (−$10.3B), ON RRP effectively empty at $0.2B, SOFR 3.63% and orderly. No funding stress anywhere — which sharpens the week's lesson: with the RRP buffer gone, the marginal absorber of long-duration supply is price, and the 30Y spent the week proving it.

concept_unit: Unit 1 · Yield curve mechanics · segment 3 of ~10
concept_title: Naming the move: steepeners, flatteners, and what each one says
concept_html: Analysts compress every curve move into a two-word name: which way yields went (bull = down, bear = up, from the bondholder's view) and what the slope did (steepener = long end moved more, flattener = front end moved more, or the long end moved toward the front). This week was a full specimen set. Monday: a bear steepener — long yields up, front end pinned, 2s10s widening to +52bp — the market demanding more term premium, the most uncomfortable move for equities. Wednesday: a bull flattener from the long end — 30Y −9bp on the buyback news while the 2Y sat still, slope back to +46bp. Thursday: the bear steepener returned in miniature (+4bp long, slope +50bp). Each name is a sentence about who moved: when the front end drives, the market is re-voting on the Fed; when the long end drives — as it did all week — the vote is about premium and supply, with the Fed a spectator. The 2Y's total range this week: zero. That is how you know which regime you are in.
client_translation: "All the drama in bonds this week happened in 20- and 30-year paper — short rates never moved. That means markets aren't arguing about what the Fed does next; they're arguing about what it costs to lend the government money for decades."
client_lens_html:
• "Walmart was down 9% — is the consumer rolling over?" — The honest answer is "one flagship datapoint, actively being tested": Walmart printed its slowest sales growth in six years, but the same week Estée Lauder beat and raised and Deere's construction business grew 18%. The system's open test (CL-0004) resolves within the week — the conversation is "here's what would confirm it," not a verdict.
  • "Moderna went up 177% and then dropped 24% — should we chase it?" — A ready-made lesson in binary outcomes: both moves are the same phenomenon — a market repricing a coin that already landed, then arguing about the payout. Position size before the flip is the only decision an investor actually controls.
  • "Why do long bond funds keep swinging?" — The 30Y went 5.31 → 5.19 → 5.23 in three sessions on term premium, a Treasury buyback, and one hot factory survey. Short-duration holdings slept through all of it — a concrete week to explain why duration, not "bonds," is the risk decision.
